candidates.title: Voluntary action queue with explicit release and recovery
candidates.proposal:
Source: the consent-based action queue. Preserve explicit acceptance, one active action per person initially, completion criteria, due dates, owner updates and a rotating willing recorder. The change is an everyday procedure for interrupted commitments: withdrawing or becoming unreachable must not leave an action apparently owned indefinitely.

Use the final eight minutes of each 45-minute meeting to review and accept actions in shared notes. A volunteer can decline, negotiate or release an accepted task without finding a replacement. On release, they leave any usable work and the next required step in the row. The recorder marks it uncommitted; responsibility transfers only when another volunteer explicitly accepts a stated deliverable and due date. The recorder maintains visibility but does not inherit execution.

If an owner supplies no update by the next weekly review, the committee marks delivery uncertain and does not assume the work will arrive. It chooses to defer dependent commitments, reduce scope or invite a replacement. Before replacement work starts, the original commitment must be explicitly released or suspended in the meeting notes to prevent duplicate execution. A returning owner checks that status before resuming. Time-sensitive actions that cannot tolerate this weekly recovery interval need a separately accepted earlier check or must remain uncommitted.

This requires only shared notes, personal calendar reminders and willingness to stop relying on uncertain delivery. Compared with the original queue, it could reduce stranded actions and chair chasing, but adds handoff work and may delay urgent tasks. It cannot replace missing capacity or expertise.
candidates.experiment: A consenting trial keeper records a four-week comparison between this recovery procedure and the original queue on comparable, low-risk actions, allocated before outcomes are known. Both use willing owners, original due dates and completion criteria. Track delivery by the original date, substantive rework or reopening within seven days, and each volunteer’s execution, administration and chasing minutes, including recorder and chair time. Report unclaimed, suspended and abandoned decisions separately. Inspect whether released work actually receives an accepting replacement and whether duplicate work occurs. Stop replacement starts immediately if ownership is disputed; defer the action until resolved. Drop the added procedure if its handoff burden exceeds useful recovered delivery. Allow seven days after the month for final rework observation; without interruptions, its recovery benefit remains uncertain.

candidates.title: Delegated action mandates that expire when key facts change
candidates.proposal:
Source: delegate execution choices when the decision is made. Preserve a consenting owner, due date, deliverable, explicit execution boundaries, independent action within those boundaries and committee review of departures. Add a narrow validity condition where changed facts could make authorized execution inappropriate.

Within the existing seven-minute mandate allocation in each 45-minute meeting, the owner and committee identify at most one material assumption for a consequential action—for example, that an advertised venue remains confirmed. Record an observable invalidating event and an authorized response: omit the affected claim, use an already approved alternative, or pause the affected part. This does not authorize new spending, policy or external commitments. Members may decline ownership; unaccepted work remains uncommitted.

The owner checks the condition at the existing point of irreversible execution, such as immediately before sending the announcement, rather than conducting recurring checks. If the assumption fails, the owner records the evidence and performs only the agreed response. If that response cannot work, they preserve completed work, pause the affected part and place the exact unresolved choice in the next meeting’s notes. The chair is not the default approver. Where no cheap, reliable validity check exists, use the ordinary collective approval process for that action.

This requires notes, calendar reminders and a committee able to delegate the relevant choices. Compared with the original mandate, it could prevent confidently executing a stale decision while retaining routine independence. Its extra check and possible waiting are worthwhile only where a changed fact would materially affect the result; most small actions need no added condition.
candidates.experiment: A willing trial keeper compares ordinary mandates with validity-conditioned mandates on comparable eligible actions over one month. Record approval-waiting days, delivery of the original intended result by its original deadline, substantive rework within seven days, and every volunteer’s specification, checking, execution and coordination minutes. Include chair interventions, pauses and reduced outcomes. Inspect whether recorded evidence justified each response and whether paused work received a committee decision. Suspend delegation for a category after an unauthorized consequential commitment; return it to collective approval. Remove conditions that repeatedly trigger unnecessary pauses. Retain the addition only if avoided mistakes or improved delivery justify checking and waiting costs. Observe final rework for seven further days; few changed assumptions may leave the benefit unresolved.

candidates.title: Replace an existing obligation when accepting a new priority
candidates.proposal:
The new mechanism is workload substitution: at the moment the committee chooses new work, it explicitly removes competing committee work. The causal lever is reducing demand, rather than improving reminders, handoffs or execution authority.

Reserve seven minutes within each 45-minute meeting for priority trades. For a proposed action, record its useful result, completion criterion and desired date. Invite a willing owner, who may decline. If that volunteer lacks time, ask which existing committee obligation could be cancelled, reduced or deferred enough to make the new action feasible. The committee may change only work within its authority; the volunteer decides whether the released capacity is sufficient. Acceptance creates one owner and a due date. Without both a feasible trade and willing acceptance, defer or reject the new action.

Record the displaced work and its consequence beside the new commitment, including any calendar change. The existing owner must acknowledge the change before anyone treats their capacity as released. If cancellation would break an external commitment or an essential dependency, the trade is unavailable until an authorized person resolves it; the new action stays uncommitted. A rotating willing recorder captures decisions, while owners manage execution and reminders. At the next meeting, inspect the new output and whether the displaced work actually stopped. If it continued, reduce or defer the new commitment instead of asking the chair to chase harder.

This needs only shared notes, a calendar and authority to stop some committee work. Compared with merely limiting each person’s active-action count, it addresses recurring duties and unfinished obligations that remain outside the queue. It could improve completion by freeing real time, but sacrifices other outcomes and may simply expose that every obligation is essential. It cannot free time controlled by employers, families or outside organizations.
candidates.experiment: For four weeks, a consenting trial keeper records all proposed actions and uses workload substitution for overloaded volunteers; compare with similar actions accepted through the simple voluntary queue without an explicit trade. Do not manufacture overload for comparison. Track original-deadline completion, seven-day substantive rework, and every member’s meeting, execution and coordination minutes, including chair time. Also record proposals declined, displaced outputs lost or delayed, and whether promised time was actually released. Inspect these consequences weekly so improved completion cannot conceal abandoned valuable work. Stop a trade immediately if it threatens an external obligation or essential dependency; restore that obligation and defer the new action. Keep the mechanism only if delivered priorities justify the displaced value and burden. Allow seven extra days to observe rework; self-selection and small numbers limit the comparison.
